title: Module 6 · Lesson 2 — Agentic RAG and knowledge graphs

lines: Single-shot RAG assumes the question is a good search query, and that one retrieval is enough.
Both often fail, so agentic retrieval is the standard upgrade.

say.0: Single-shot rag assumes the question is a good search query, and that one retrieval is enough.

lines: Meet Maya, an analyst at a bicycle maker, using the company assistant.
She asks what the warranty says about cracked frames, and gets a great answer.
Then she types: and what about the carbon one?
Searched literally, that phrase matches nothing useful.
So the agent first rewrites the query, resolving the carbon one from the chat history.
It also splits compound questions and tries paraphrases.
Next, it picks the right source: product docs, ticket history, a SQL database, or the web.
It doesn't always hit the same index.

say.0: Next, it picks the right source: product docs, ticket history, a sequel database, or the web.

lines: Before answering, it grades the results: do they actually answer the question?
If not, it rewrites the query and retrieves again.
This grade, rewrite, retry loop is the single most valuable addition.
Cap it at two or three rounds, then answer with what you have, or say you can't.
Now Maya asks which suppliers of parts in the recalled batch also ship to EU plants.
No single chunk holds that answer: it's a join across documents.
One fix is iterative decomposition: find the recalled parts, then their suppliers, then where they ship.
Each hop's result shapes the next search.
The other is GraphRAG: extract entities and relations into a graph up front.
Then the join becomes a graph traversal instead of a similarity search.

say.0: The other is graph rag: extract entities and relations into a graph up front.

lines: But a graph needs a big extraction pipeline and ongoing upkeep.
It pays off only when multi-hop, relational questions are the core workload.
Finally, Maya asks how many frames were returned last quarter.
That lives in a database, so the agent writes SQL rather than searching embedded rows.

say.1: That lives in a database, so the agent writes sequel rather than searching embedded rows.

lines: Guard text-to-SQL with a restricted schema, read-only credentials, validated queries, row limits, and timeouts.
And return the SQL with the answer so it can be checked.

say.0: Guard text-to-sequel with a restricted schema, read-only credentials, validated queries, row limits, and timeouts.

lines: Exam tip: say knowledge graph only when explicit relationships must be traversed, like supply chains.
For find-the-passage questions it's over-engineering, so read on for the details.
